reasoning_traces.think:
The core insight is that learning, whether trial-and-error or inventive, is fundamentally about modifying cognitive gestalts—structured perceptions or problem representations. Transfer experiments quantify how one problem's resolution affects another’s solvability through a recognition potential \( \mathcal{R} \). This potential is influenced by the gestalt-inducing similarity \( \mathcal{G} \) between problems. A positive transfer implies \( \Delta \mathcal{R} > 0 \), suggesting that prior experience facilitates recognition of subsequent solutions. Conversely, negative transfer implies \( \Delta \mathcal{R} < 0 \), indicating interference. These phenomena are modeled as \( \mathcal{L}_{\text{transfer}} = \text{sgn}(\Delta \mathcal{R}) \cdot \mathcal{G} \), where \( \mathcal{G} \) captures the structural alignment between problems. The dual nature of learning—both as a modification of existing gestalts and as an evolution toward new ones—is captured by the interplay of \( \mathcal{G} \) and \( \mathcal{R} \). Failure modes occur when \( \mathcal{G} \to 0 \) (no structural overlap) or when \( \mathcal{R} \to 0 \) (solution not accessible).
